item.title: Timeless Mechanics
item.description:
Hello Newton

This semester I’m taking Michael Esfeld’s course on the philosophy of physics at EPFL, and I wanted to talk about one idea I found interesting.

I will try to keep the philosophy to a minimum since it’s not the main point I want to discuss.

Essentially when Newton established his laws of motion, he needed an absolute space and time to exist by themselves independently of the objects in the universe.

As a physical theory it works great, but some people (namely, Leibniz) had issues with the ontology it proposes. The ontology of a theory is basically all the things that exist independetly of everything else. A good ontology should not have more things than what is absolutelly neccesary to explain the phenomena we observe (this is called parsimony).

Hello Leibniz

Leibniz argued that in Newton’s view (substantivalism), configurations that were rotated or translated with respect to this absolute space could not be distinguished and behave just the same, even if they are two different configurations of the universe. The same goes for time and velocity, if every event in the universe happened 5 seconds later or with a constant velocity, we still have no way of telling the difference.

In Leibniz’s view (relationalism), you only really need the distances between objects and the order of configurations. The thing is that nowhere in this ontology it says how long things take, only in what order they happen. This seems strange at first since it doesn’t fit with our experience of the world and it doesn’t even let us use the concept of velocities.

I don’t want to get into the arguments for or against this, but from a physics standpoint it actually is possible to write Newtonian mechanics in a way that only uses these two things, and time and velocity come out of it as derived concepts. Let’s get into it.

Paths in configuration space

Take the universe as particles with masses at positions . A configuration of the whole universe is a single point in a -dimensional space, which we call configuration space. A history of the universe is then a path through this space. We have a sequence of configurations and an order, nothing more.

Analytical mechanics and Jacobi’s principle

For this part some basic knowledge of analytical mechanics will be needed.

We know from analytical mechanics that physical trajectories make stationary a scalar quantity known as the action. In its standard form (Hamilton’s principle) it is written as an integral over time, with the kinetic energy and the potential energy:

where we compare all paths that go between two configurations in the same time . There is an alternative formulation (Maupertuis’ principle) that compares paths with equal energy instead of equal time.The stationary quantiy is now the abbreviated action:

But we still haven’t got rid of time, since . But now look at the term in the integrand, we can substitute and get the kinetic energy T:

Multiplying again by and noticing that we get:

The right hand side now doesn’t depend on time at all, and with it we can define the length of an infinitesimal step along our path in configuration space:

Intuitively we can think of as a replacement of that instead of time measures change in configuration space (its just a sum of displacements ).

Putting everything together,

Everything that depends on time is now gone and we have Jacobi’s principle. Every trajectory in the universe can be calculated using this and the principle of least action, whithout mentioning time.

Why the label doesn’t matter

To actually calculate anything along a path, we need to label the points with some parameter . Since we don’t have time, can be any increasing function.

The action of any given path is just a line integral, and if you’ve taken a vector calculus course you’ll know that it’s value won’t depend on the parametrization:

Written out with a parameter , using , the action becomes

is what the kinetic energy would be if were time. It is not physical, since it changes if we relabel the path, but the combination doesn’t.

Where time comes from

Making stationary gives the equations of motion. With , the Lagrangian is , and the Euler–Lagrange equations say

Only depends on the velocities, with , and only depends on the positions.

They look messy, but notice that the same factor appears on both sides (inverted on the left). This suggests choosing a new label that absorbs it:

With this label the momentum becomes , and the equations of motion become

which is Newton’s second law. Any other label would leave extra terms in the equations, so is the unique label (up to choosing units and a starting point) in which the law takes its simplest form. We call it time.

Not so surprinsing

It is not surprising that we arrive at newton’s laws, since the analytical mechanics concepts we borrowed were built explicitely to produce them. The point is that instead of taking time as fundamental we can take the Jacobi action as fundamental and derive time from it.

In my daily life I will likely still use Newton’s laws, but it’s a nice example of how math alone can’t tell us how the universe really is. These two formalisms produce equivalent predictions but have very different philosophical implications.

This will change a bit when we try to remove absolute space, but I will leave that for another post.

item.title: Flip-Flopping Claude spinner verbs
item.description:
Spinner verbs

Whenever you ask Claude a question, a little spinner appears while it thinks and next to it some word like “Discombobulating”, “Crystallizing”, or “Moonwalking”. These are “spinner verbs”, in total there are 187 different ones. Basically their role is to have something entertaining while you wait instead of it just saying “Loading…”

Some other examples are Simmering, Flummoxing, Watchamacalliting, Dilly-dallying, Bebopping, Meandering, Spelunking, Orbiting, Transmuting, Quantumizing etc etc.

The thing is that they all share a similar style even though they can be about very different things. “Simmering” and “Quantumizing” have nothing in common in meaning but they feel right. “Loading” or “Running” would feel wrong even though they describe what Claude is actually doing.

In this post we will explore a method for proposing new verbs like these using word embeddings and some basic data science.

Word embeddings

If we want to analyze these verbs we need a way to represent them mathematically. For this we use word embeddings. A word embedding represents a word as a list of numbers, which we can interpret as vectors. A neural network reads enormous amounts of text and assigns those coordinates so that words used in similar ways land near each other. For example, it notices that “dog”, “puppy” and “cat” appear in similar sentences and puts them close together, while “dog” and “volcano” end up far apart. Distance works now as a measure of similarity (see Annex A), and once words are points in space we can work with their meaning using simple geometry and linear algebra. For example we can find neighbours, group into themes with clusters of points, or find regions where certain words live.

Here we use all-mpnet-base-v2, an open sentence embedding model that turns each word into a 768-dimension vector that we normalize to length one (see Annex A).

Also, here we are working with 768-dimensional geometry, so some of our intuition about distances doesn’t necessarily translate (see post Everybody lives in Ecuador for a discussion of this). For some things it’s the same, but for example the angle between two random vectors is usually almost , so if two vectors have an angle of between them it means that they are actually much more similar than we would think, living in a 3D world.

Candidate verbs

For the candidates we take 9,000 gerunds from WordNet (see Annex F), and for the spinner verbs we use the list of 187 verbs that Claude uses. We embed all of them and run a vibe-check to eliminate negative verbs. Since the spinner verbs appear in a the screen while we wait, it would be weird to have a verb that is negative or violent.

How do we do this? We can take advantage of how embeddings work. We measure the distance between each candidate and several “positive” words (delightful, playful, cozy, etc) and several “negative” words (violent, disease, manipulative, etc). If a candidate is closer to the negative words than the positive words we discard it (see Annex B). This eliminates about 1,500 candidates, some of which would have otherwise been good spinner verbs. For example, “Conspiring”, “Force-feeding”, and ironically “Hallucinating”.

We could now be tempted calculate the average embedding of the spinner verbs, and find the candidates closest to that average verb. This does not work. There are many themes in the spinner verbs, for example cooking (“Simmering”, “Sautéeing”, “Marinating”, “Braising”) or physics (“Ionizing”, “Crystalizing”, “Quantumizing”). If we just took the average, it would fall somewhere in the middle but not close to any single one. But first, we need a way to evaluate if a candidate would make a good spinner verb or not.

Evaluating candidates

To evaluate how good a candidate is we run a logistic regression model trained on the spinner verbs’ embeddings and 8 features (length, rarity, rare letters, etc) (see Annex C). We can then give a score to each candidate and rank them (see Annex C). Using this method words like “Brainstorming”, “Formulating”, and “Stirring” get top scores while words like “Hazing”, “Court-martialing”, and “Chain-smoking” fall to the bottom. So far so good.

It’s interesting how most of the worst candidates are hyphenated while also many good candidates are hyphenated (flip-flopping, teeter-tottering). Out of the official spinner verbs, the hyphenated ones have some kind of rhyme or repetition (Dilly-dallying, Razzle-dazzling) so the model learned (see Annex C) that a hyphen alone is bad (which is a very clear indicator) but a hyphen with repetition is good.

My personal favorite is Leapfrogging since it has a funny vibe and also references the leapfrog symplectic integrator.

Some other ones I liked are Oscillating, Somersaulting, Whizzing, Weaving, Twiddling, and Scintillating.

In this search bar you can type any word and see how good it is (see Annex C). It also tells you if it is an official spinner verb, closest spinner verb, and whether or not it passed the vibe check.

viewof query = Inputs.text({placeholder: "Try Knitting, Moonwalking, Hallucinating…", label: "Search a word"})
query.trim().length < 2
  ? html`<p style="color:#52514e;">Type at least two letters. The list has ${words.length.toLocaleString("en")} words.</p>`
  : matches.length
    ? html`${matches.map(card)}`
    : html`<p style="color:#52514e;">"${query}" is not among the ${words.length.toLocaleString("en")} words: it may be an invented word, a non-verb, or removed by the safety blocklist.</p>`
words = (await FileAttachment("word_scores.csv").csv()).map(d => ({
  ...d, pct: +d.pct, closeness: +d.closeness,
  key: d.word.toLowerCase(), lemmaKey: d.lemma.toLowerCase()
}))

matches = {
  const q = query.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (q.length < 2) return [];
  const exact = words.filter(d => d.key === q || d.lemmaKey === q);
  const starts = words.filter(d => !exact.includes(d) && d.key.startsWith(q));
  const inside = words.filter(d => !exact.includes(d) && !starts.includes(d) && d.key.includes(q));
  return [...exact, ...starts, ...inside].slice(0, 6);
}

statusText = ({
  "official": "Official spinner verb (scored while hidden from the model)",
  "candidate": "Candidate",
  "failed the vibe check": "Candidate, but failed the vibe check",
  "British spelling": "Filtered: British spelling of an American form",
  "removed by Anthropic": "Was an official verb, later removed by Anthropic",
  "same verb as an official one": "Filtered: another form of an official verb",
  "removed by hand": "Filtered by hand (veto list)"
})

topText = p => {
  const t = (1 - p) * 100;
  return t < 1 ? `top ${Math.max(t, 0.1).toFixed(1)}%` : t <= 50 ? `top ${t.toFixed(0)}%` : `bottom ${(100 - t).toFixed(0)}%`;
}

card = d => html`<div style="border:1px solid #e4e3df;border-radius:8px;padding:10px 14px;margin:8px 0;">
  <div style="display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:baseline;gap:12px;">
    <strong style="font-size:1.15em;">${d.word}</strong>
    <span><strong>${topText(d.pct)}</strong> <span style="color:#52514e;">(score ${(100 * d.pct).toFixed(1)} / 100)</span></span>
  </div>
  <div style="background:#eeede9;border-radius:4px;height:8px;margin:6px 0 8px;">
    <div style="width:${(100 * d.pct).toFixed(1)}%;background:${d.status === "official" ? "#2a78d6" : "#eb6834"};height:8px;border-radius:4px;"></div>
  </div>
  <div style="color:#52514e;font-size:0.92em;line-height:1.5;">
    ${statusText[d.status]}${d.note ? html` · <strong>${d.note}</strong>` : ""}<br>
    Closest theme: ${d.theme} · Closest official verb: ${d.nearest} (closeness ${d.closeness.toFixed(2)})
  </div>
</div>`

Clustering and themes

Another way to find good candidates is to identify the themes we already talked about and find candidates that fit into those themes. Using Ward clustering we divide the 187 spinner verbs into 15 groups (see Annex D). Then, from each group we find the candidates with the highest score that lie inside that region (see Annex D). This gives us a list of good candidates that also fit inside the existing themes. Here are some examples.

My favorite is Eddyng since it fits the swirly theme, is fun to say, and is related to physics (eddy currents, eddy viscosity, etc).

New themes

We can also try to find new themes to add. For example, we can look at words that score highly but are not close to any existing cluster (see Annex E). These words score highly because of their style and not because they have similar meaning to the spinner verbs.

Again we see some propositions.

Out of these my favorites are Slaloming, Circumnavigating, and Shimmering.

Annex

A. From a word to a vector

Model. sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2: a transformer encoder (MPNet) fine-tuned so that sentences with similar meaning get nearby vectors. Its output for a piece of text is the average of its token vectors (mean pooling), a vector in .

Carrier sentences. The encoder is trained on sentences, and a bare word like “Baking” is ambiguous (a verb? an adjective?). So each word is fed to the encoder in 5 short templates:

“{w}”, “{w}…”, “Claude is {w}.”, “The assistant is busy {w}.”, “Please wait while I finish {w}.”

The 5 vectors are averaged. The shared sentence part is roughly the same for every word, so it mostly cancels out in comparisons, and what is left is the word as an activity in progress.

Normalisation. The average is scaled to length one,

Distance and closeness. For unit vectors, the (Euclidean) distance and the dot product carry the same information: Small distance means large dot product. Throughout the post (and in the search box) “closeness” is (between and ; in practice 0.2 to 0.9 here). Ranking words by distance or by closeness gives the same order.

B. Vibe check

Anchors. 8 pleasant anchors : delightful, playful, cozy, whimsical, cheerful, gentle, curious, charming. 14 unpleasant anchors : violent, sexual, disease, illness, cruel, creepy, manipulative, bodily fluids, medical procedure, harassment, death, insulting, disgusting, deceitful. They are embedded like any other word.

Vibe value.

Threshold. The bar is not zero. It is set by Anthropic’s own list: a candidate must be at least as pleasant as the 1st percentile of the 187 official verbs (). So the bar is calibrated on what Anthropic was happy to ship (their least pleasant verbs are Garnishing, Osmosing, Booping). Because the bar is slightly below zero, it is a little more lenient than the simple rule in the main text (“closer to the negative words than to the positive ones”).

C. Logistic regression

Labels. The 187 official verbs are labelled 1. Every other candidate is labelled 0.

A label 0 doesn’t necessarily mean it’s a bad spinner verb, just that we don’t know if it is. This setting is called positive–unlabelled learning. The scores are then not true probabilities, but the ranking is still meaningful, and the ranking is all we use.

Input. For each word, : the embedding plus 8 standardised features:

Model. Here and minimise the weighted log-loss plus an L2 penalty: We use (chosen by cross-validation from 0.3, 1, 3, 10). The weights are “balanced” (), so the 187 positives count as much as the thousands of negatives. The score shown in the post is the percentile of . Official verbs are scored while hidden from the model (see below).

Does it work? We hide part of the official verbs and check where the model ranks them among the hidden candidates.

The 40% (the share of hidden official verbs that land in the top 5%) doesn’t seem too good, but it is 8x better than chance, and the median hidden verb falls in the 91st percentile of the hidden words. Also, 187 positive labels are not that many, and many of the words that beat them can also genuinely be good spinner verbs, so the model is not wrong to rank them high.

D. Ward clustering and maximal relevance

Ward clustering. Start with each of the 187 verbs as its own cluster. At every step, merge the two clusters whose merge increases the total within-cluster spread the least: where is the mean vector of cluster . This favours compact, similar-sized groups. Stopping at clusters gives the themes. We chose by the silhouette score over (the silhouette compares how close each verb is to its own group with how close it is to the next group. higher is better).

Centroid. A theme’s centre is the mean of its members’ vectors, rescaled to length one: .

Does a candidate fit a theme? Each candidate goes to its closest centre, but closest is not the same as close. A word far from everything would still be forced into the least-far theme. So a candidate is allowed into theme only if In words, it must be as close to the centre as all but the 5% least central official verbs of that theme. The cap 0.72 (the median closeness of all official verbs to their own centre) stops a tiny theme of near-synonyms from rejecting good fits just because the others are much closer. The candidate must also be in the model’s top 15% best scoring verbs.

The catch-all theme. For example the theme containing (Accomplishing, Doing, but also Cascading, Enchanting, Razzle-dazzling) collects the official verbs that fit no sharper theme. So its centre is almost the average of all candidates (closeness 0.93 to that average, against 0.63 for the most specific theme), and it is the closest theme for 31% of all candidates. For this theme, “close to the centre” just means “a generic verb”, which is why its proposals (Genuflecting, Exhilarating, Dovetailing) are weak. This shows that the method is not perfect.

Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR). Among the 80 best-scoring candidates that fit, we pick up to 8 one at a time. Each pick is where is the score stretched so that the worst clean candidate is 0 and the best is 1, and the words already picked. The second term punishes a word for being too close to one already picked, so we don’t get five synonyms of Simmering.

E. Finding new themes

  1. Keep the top 6% of candidates by score.
  2. Keep only the words that fail the fit test of Annex D for all 15 themes: good words that belong nowhere (113 words).
  3. Group them with Ward clustering.
  4. Keep a group only if it has at least 4 words and is tight enough.

Tightness is the average closeness of a group’s words to the group’s centre (its normalised mean vector, as in Annex D). Anthropic’s own 15 themes range from 0.64 to 0.77 (plus 0.89 for a tiny theme of four trans- synonyms). A new theme needs at least 0.76, i.e. it must be tighter than 13 of the 15 real themes. With a stricter bar (0.80) only Sparkles, Needlework and Spins & turns survive, with a looser one, groups without a clear theme appear.

F. Building the candidate list

  • Sources. Every WordNet verb turned into its -ing form (with lemminflect), plus every -ing word in the wordfreq English list that comes from a real verb. Hyphenated verbs are kept (flip-flop, dilly-dally), so that a hyphen alone does not give away “spinner verb”.

  • Size. 9,016 words in total (8,992 real English words + 24 official coinages like Clauding). After removing official verbs, British spellings, the vibe check and the veto, 6,741 candidates can be proposed.

item.title: On the ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
item.description:
What is Go

Lately I’ve been playing some Go with my friend Juan (not myself). Go is a Chinese board game where you basically have to place stones on a grid to capture territory. A group of stones is captured when it loses all its liberties (the empty points adjacent to it) i.e. when it is completely surrounded by enemy stones. As the nerds we are, we quickly noticed some similarities between the game of Go and the Ising model for ferromagnetism.

What is the Ising model

The Ising model is a model for ferromagnetism developed in the 1920s. Essentially, it treats a material as a grid of tiny magnets (spins) that can point either up or down. The probability of finding the material in a given configuration (some combination of up and down spins) depends on its energy, which depends on two things (more in Annex A): 1. the external magnetic field, which pushes every spin in its direction, and 2. the interaction between neighbouring spins. When neighbours prefer to point the same way, the spins can align on their own, even without an external field, and the material is ferromagnetic.

The similarities lie in the fact that liberties in Go are like spin coupling in the Ising model (your orthogonal neighbours affect whether you stay alive or not), territory can be white/black like spins are up/down, and that you end up with blocks of territory (lonely pieces die).

Also, I’m sadly (and obviously) not the first person to ever make this connection (see Stern et al., 2004, or Alvarado et al., 2017).

The model

I now set out to describe predicting the outcome of Go games with this model, and hopefully try to see if it makes sense to define some notion of ferromagnetism for the game.

Grosso modo this is the solution we will use: start from a given position, and treat the existing stones as an external magnetic field. Then, with that external field, compute the probability distribution of an Ising model and take the prediction of the final outcome as the expected spins.

Essentially what we want is to find the parameters that assign low energies to the real final territory given some position and high energies to the rest.

This model has three main things to be learned: how the color of a stone affects the external magnetic field around it (), how the position in the board affects the external magnetic field (), and finally the coupling between neighbours (). How many parameters? is a 5x5 kernel, is a 9x9 map (the entire board), and is a 3x3 kernel. However from symmetry we can reduce this to 6 parameters for , 15 parameters for , and 2 for . Total 23. The next step is to find a dataset to train these parameters, and based on the shape of we will be able to see if Go can be described through ferromagnetic coupling.

To build the training set I downloaded the KataGo model and made it play about 7000 games against itself, from which I extracted a position in the middle of the game and the final territory assigned once the game was done. Then I trained the parameters with PyTorch to maximize the log likelihood of the final territory in all the games given the model parameters (see Annex B).

Once we have the trained parameters we can compare what the model predicts will be the outcome (see Annex C) given a starting position and compare it to the actual outcome.

This doesn’t seem too bad, but let’s take a look at the parameters. The first thing is that the baseline with no spin coupling already does fairly well, so it’s not immediately clear whether or not coupling is really needed.

From the coupling parameters we also see that only orthogonal neighbours couple, which makes sense given the rules of the game.

In numbers, both models get about 80 % of the points right, so the coupling doesn’t help to guess each point. Where it does help is with the whole board at once: the log-loss of the real final territory is cut in half, because the model knows that territory comes in blocks.

And is a strong coupling, the textbook 2D Ising model (infinite board, no external field) orders into a magnet above . Our board is small and the stones act as a field so this is only a rough reference, but it is something.

The coupling also changes how the stones create a field. Without coupling the kernel is a broad blob with large weights even far from the center. Every square is guessed on its own, so a stone has to spread its colour over its whole area of influence by itself. With coupling the kernel is very local and even has a negative weight on its four orthogonal neighbours.

The bias is small and noisy but we can recognise some areas and positions that vaguely make sense knowing the game. Again a big change between coupling and non-coupling cases.

Also, the average predictions with and without coupling look very similar, but that’s only the average. If instead we sample two possible endings from each model for the same game they change a lot.

Without coupling every point is drawn on its own while with coupling you get blobs of the same color like in a real game.

Ferromagnetism?

Of course Go is not Ising. A group lives or dies all at once, a stone that will be captured pushes the wrong way, shape matters and not just the number of stones, our domain is really small, etc etc… Our analogy ends here.

But we can forget about these silly limitations and imagine a hypothetical where the game of Go was just our fitted Ising model. Would it be ferromagnetic?

Let’s see two ways to find a ferromagnet.

  1. Heat it up and at some critical temperature it loses its magnetization, with a peak in the susceptibility (how much the magnetization responds to small changes).

  2. Below if you add an external field and then remove it, it stays magnetized (hysteresis). Our model has no temperature, but we can give it one by dividing the energy by so that is the trained model (details in Annex D).

Let’s start without stones on an empty board (no external field).

There is a clear peak at , and our model () sits below it, so with no external field it is already magnetized.

And it has memory. After a push and back to zero field it stays 95 % magnetized, while above () it just follows the field and forgets it. So the coupling the model learned from Go is, on its own, the coupling of a magnet.

Again this is not surprising knowing the coupling kernel from the training, but it still learnt that all on its own from looking at games. It could have also learnt a different coupling or no coupling at all.

The answer

Yes, but not exactly.

To end the post here’s a whole game move by move with its corresponding prediction at each point.

Notice how with few stones (small external field) the whole board leans towards one color like in the empty board case. It starts to get good around the middle (trained on mid-games). Also, towards the end it doesn’t realize the white pieces A4-A5-A6 were dead from the start. Still, it looks nice.

Annex

A. The model

Each point of the board has a spin , its final owner, seen from the player to move ( for the player to move, for the opponent). Neutral points are left out. The position is (own stone, opponent stone, empty). The model is

where is the partition function, a sum over configurations. The temperature is absorbed in the parameters (). The field is a convolution of the stones with a kernel plus a bias per square. is for orthogonal neighbours, for diagonal ones and otherwise.

All parameters are invariant under the 8 symmetries of the board. That leaves 6 values for , 15 for and 2 for , 23 in total.

If all spins but one are fixed,

B. Training

The negative log-likelihood per point is minimized over the 5535 training games,

where is the same sum restricted to the configurations that agree with the real owners. The exponent is linear in , so is convex.

This is a transfer matrix: a vector of 512 entries multiplied 9 times by the matrix and the diagonal factors . The product is done in log space to avoid overflow. The gradient comes from PyTorch, and LBFGS converges in a few minutes. was checked against the brute-force sum on and boards. On there would be 8192 states per column, so this only works for small boards.

C. Prediction

The prediction is the magnetization of each point, , and . It is computed exactly as , differentiating the transfer matrix computation with PyTorch.

item.title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
item.description:
Pick a point uniformly at random in the unit ball of . For high enough this point will practically always fall along the surface, i.e. high-dimensional watermelons have no red part. But not only that, this is also true for the equators of high-dimensional spheres. Let’s see why.

Warm-up: the surface

First: a random point in the unit ball is practically always near its surface. Since we choose the point uniformly at random, the chance of being near the surface is the same as the volume of a thin shell of width near the surface. Like an onion.

Shrinking the unit ball by a factor gives exactly , and shrinking multiplies volumes by once per coordinate, so

For and the inner part holds of the volume, for it holds and for it holds . The rest lies in the thin shell near the surface.

If we sample points, their distance to the center has density (the derivative of ), and as grows it gets closer and closer to .

Setup for the equator

Now let’s define what equator means. For a given unit vector , the equator is the hyperplane , and the latitude of a point is its coordinate . Being close to the equator means having for some .

In the equator of a sphere () is a circle (), which feels like a very small part. But in the equator of is an . It only loses one dimension out of , and in losing one dimension out of a hundred million may not matter as much.

Slices and slabs

Where does the random point’s latitude tend to land? It falls between and with probability proportional to the volume of the thin slab of the ball. The slab is approximately an -dimensional ball of radius with thickness , so its volume is proportional to . Hence the latitude has density

where is some function of (we don’t care). We will use it shortly. Also, be careful, the diagram is in 3D but the calculation is for an arbitrary number of dimensions .
